segs: A L I F E W I T H O U T SO U L 1
A LIFE WITHOUT
SOUL
RICK JAMES
There are two types of people in the world. (A good
way to begin an article as you’re compelled to see what
kind of asinine over-generalization or false dichotomy
could possibly follow.) There are those who believe
that inside every person is a soul or spiritual
dimension, and there are those who believe that the
only thing deep inside us is our intestines.
Consider the phenomenon of “the enduring sense of
self.” Your cells are ceaselessly dying and replicating.
You no longer possess the same cells you had at birth,
yet you have a cohesive sense that you are still you.
Therefore, “You” are not simply your cells.
Remember when Millhouse bought Bart’s soul for
$5—boy, that was a scary episode. Bart’s soul, if you
remember, was a translucent Bart. Philosophically, all
that is meant by a soul is a non-material or spiritual
aspect of who we are: something that cannot be seen
under a microscope or lava lamp and most likely
survives our physical deaths. Unlike Bart’s soul, it is
doubtful that a disembodied soul has any appearance
whatsoever, for any appearance, even a translucent
one, constitutes a body. But as the cartooning of Bart
is outsourced overseas to cell animators getting paid
a chicken’s egg for a day’s wages we cannot be overly
critical. And with that social criticism we will now
turn to the evidence for a soul.
Or what about the objectivity of the self: you
distinguish yourself from your experiences and
emotions. When you squash a fly, there’s no reason to
conclude that its experience is separate from itself. In
other words, in its tiny fly brain, it senses, “I am pain”
(if it does feel pain). You, on the other hand, distinctly
feel that pain is happening to you and that you are
distinct from the experience of pain. The same could
be said of emotions: when I’m enraged, I feel that a
mood has overtaken me, but I am distinct from the
mood; I might even try to fight off the mood or act as
though it is not effecting me. And then there is PMS…
(What do you think I’m nuts? I’m already offending
half the populace arguing for a soul.) The point being,
“You” cannot be distilled down to simply feelings or
emotions.
INADEQUACY OF A PURELY PHYSICAL VIEW
The person who does not believe in a non-material
(read spiritual) component of man must explain every
human function biologically, and that’s a difficult
assignment, as noted by MIT-trained scientist Gerald
Schroeder, “Consciousness has all the trappings of a
nonreducible element of our universe. The conscious
mind is not mystical, but it may be metaphysical—
meaning out of the physical.”
Or when you are thinking about a pink elephant,
where in your brain is there an actual image of a pink
elephant? If we were to tear you apart piece by piece,
at what point would we be able to find a clump of
cells and put them under a microscope and locate the
QuickTime file of the Pink Elephant?
Furthermore, there is the “aboutness” of the mind;
it is always daydreaming, planning, remembering,
envisioning, out for a night on the town and usually
returning way past curfew. It’s as if our mind would
wander away if it weren’t tethered to our brain.
Of the many attributes of consciousness not easily
reducible to natural or biological processes we’ll
highlight just a few:
Wilder Penfield, the renowned neurosurgeon, did a
series of experiments on epileptic patients. Using

electricity, he would stimulate certain regions within
the brain, causing the patient to move his or her arm
or leg or head. The patient always knew that he or she
was not the one moving the body parts. In other words,
the patient clearly had a sense of existence apart
from the interactions between the brain and body.
Probing the entire cerebral cortex, Penfield concluded
that there was no place that could be electrically
stimulated to cause a person to believe or decide.
and immediately sat down and drew up plans for the
Pyramids.
For years people have tried to reduce humans to
nothing more than a series of drives (Freud’s life
and death drives, for example) and instincts. But
Cambridge professor C. S. Lewis proposed the
following thought experiment:
In the book The Case for a Creator, philosopher J. P.
Moreland makes the following observation: “I know
that consciousness isn’t a physical phenomenon
because there are things that are true of my
consciousness that aren’t true of anything physical.”
He goes on to give the following example:
Let’s say you heard a woman screaming. For a moment
you would sense two different instincts, says Lewis.
The first is self-preservation: get out of there as fast as
you can. The second is a herding instinct— woman in
trouble, must save (the herding instinct is primitive
and therefore doesn’t use pronouns). But what do you
choose to do, asks Lewis?
Some of my thoughts have the attribute of being
true. Tragically, some of my thoughts have the
attribute of being false. However, none of my brain
states are true or false. No scientist can look at
the state of my brain and say, “Oh, that particular
brain state is true and that one is false.” So there
is something true of my conscious states that are
not true of my brain states, and consequently they
can’t be the same thing.
Your consciousness chooses between the instincts,
and it is as different and separate from them as the
pianist is from the keys he chooses to play on the
piano. The consciousness sits over and above our
instincts, drives, and desires, and it chooses which
it will act upon. Therefore consciousness cannot be
reduced to either an instinct, drive or desire.
So difficult is the problem posed by our consciousness
that Laurence C. Wood stated that, “Many brain
scientists have been compelled to postulate the
existence of an immaterial mind, even though they
might not embrace a belief in life after death.”
It is in the face of such evidence that perhaps the
worlds most renown philosopher and atheist, Oxford
professor Antony Flew, recently changed his position
to the shock of the philosophical world, concluding
that some sort of intelligence or First Cause must
have created the universe. “A super-intelligence is
the only good explanation for the origin of life and the
complexity of nature.” (Though the succinctness of
the quote makes it seem like he was a hostage being
forced to read it)
DID OUR SOULS EVOLVE?
Strictly speaking, I am making a case for the existence
of a soul, and not where it came from. But the inability
for evolutionary theory to account for the existence of
the soul or consciousness is far from irrelevant.
A L I F E W I T H O U T SO U L 2
The ability to speak distinguishes man from all apes
and hominids. Most hominids had small, apelike
brains and no capacity for language. Then, suddenly
in the fossil record, man appears with several unique
features, including an enlarged brain capacity with no
clear-cut links between the two.
If one were to reconstruct the events of the fossil
record, it would appear that one day, Unk the
caveman, came back from a mastodon ride with
a tumor the size of a grapefruit. Upon further
inspection he found the growth to be a larger brain
giving him abilities for language and abstract thought,
NEAR DEATH EXPERIENCES
In 2001, Dutch cardiologist Dr. Pim van Lommel,
working in the Division of Cardiology at the Hospital
Rijnstate in the Netherlands, published the results
of a ten-year study, “Near-death experience in
survivors of cardiac arrest” (I’m sure the movie
title will be more compelling). In the report, Near
Death experiences were defined as “the reported
memory of all impressions during a special state of
consciousness, including specific elements such as
out-of-body experience, pleasant feelings and seeing a
tunnel, a light, a being of light, deceased relatives, or a
life review.”
In other words, patients who were clinically dead,
experienced consciousness, but not simply that: they

In an interview with Dr Pim van Lommel, he was
asked, “What could be doing the perceiving since it is
not a conscious brain, eye and ear system? This was
his answer:
to this category the billions of stories that touch
on paranormal experiences, from premonitions
concerning the future to religious visions. And while
99.9% of it is probably dribble, the sheer quantity and
universality of the experiences make it an argument
not easily dismissed. These phenomena all point
beyond our physical bodies to a mind or soul, and
perhaps point even further to an Intelligent Designer,
a First Cause, God.
Exactly, exactly. That means when there is no
activity in the brain, let’s say a flat EEG, and
people can still have their full consciousness with
cognition, emotion, with memories from their
youth, all for the possibility of perceiving. That
means [the soul] is something outside your body
that you can receive in your body by your brain.
The continuance of consciousness in the absence
of recorded brain wave activity provides powerful
evidence for the existence of a soul.
LAST THOUGHTS
If the answer to the question of who we are is “a
unique hybrid of body and soul” it really does have
profound implications. One of which may be the
answer to the second question, “Where have we come
from?” The existence of a soul clearly implicates
a Creator, as evolution speaks to biology not
metaphysics, by which I mean, it is an absurdity to
conceive of evolving a soul (non-matter).
REFLEXIVE MORALITY AND SPIRITUALITY
The spiritual and moral impulse of man is perhaps the
most epistemologically intuitive of all the indicators
of a soul. We experience that impulse in some of the
following phenomena:
Religion: People are innately religious, with over
90% of the world’s population believing in God.
Wherever you go, people instinctively pray and bow
toward heaven. It would seem that belief in God is not
something people are reasoned into, but something
they must be persuaded out of.
A L I F E W I T H O U T SO U L 3
Oughtness: Most humans have a sense that
things are not as they should be. We struggle with
circumstances, resent death, complain of evil, and
have a general sense that we were made for something
better: that things “ought” to be different. Why do we
have these thoughts? Why shouldn’t we simply accept
life on its own terms?
If the soul is a Creator’s thumbprint then the very
nature of our soul may also provide some clues to the
nature of God. We might, for example, extrapolate that
God is a moral, creative, loving, spiritual, aesthetic,
relational being. But that’s another topic. My closing
point is simply this: that all of the experiences
described seem to be pointers to the existence of a
soul, and a soul seems to be a pointer to the existence
of God, which in turn points to the stupidity of Bart
for selling his soul. And with that, I’ll stop pointing.
Morality: The Nazi’s appealed to culturally relative
morality at the Nuremburg Trials, but no one was
buying it because we intuit that no matter what the
culture, there are certain actions that are intrinsically
right and wrong. There are, most assuredly, cases
where right and wrong are culturally defined, but it
does not negate the intuitive objectivity that torturing
children and the sex slave trade are wrong no matter
who is practicing them.
